newsitem.title: USA: Doe Run confirms shutdown of Buick lead plant.
newsitem.headline: Doe Run confirms shutdown of Buick lead plant.

text.p: Doe Run confirmed Monday that a roof collapse at its Buick recycling plant will stop production for six weeks with the loss of about 6,000 short tons of secondary lead.
Doe Run president Jeff Zelms said probably the presence of some aluminum in the lead scrap that was fed into the reverberatory furnace at Buick caused it to rumble excessively.

"The rumbling caused a partial failure of the suspended roof," Zelms said. "We could have chosen to fix the roof, but since we were within sight of a shutdown for complete rebricking of the furnace, we took the decision to do it early."
Buick produced 90,000 short tons of recycled lead in the fiscal year which ended Oct 30.
With the outtage, production in the present fiscal year, starting Nov 1, will be about 85,000 short tons, Zelms added.

The furnace had been running continuously for 31 months, and Doe Run had planned to notch up 36 months before a maintenance shutdown. The normal life between rebricking is 12 to 18 months, Zelms said.
News of the outtage at Doe Run initially pushed up LME lead prices by $6 per tonne.
Zelms said Doe Run may have been a little aggressive in running the furnace for twice as long as usual between maintenance shutdowns.
A combination of a fragile roof and the need to rebrick the furance probably made the plant vulnerable in any rumbling.

"But you should not be putting aluminum in a lead bath," Zelms said. "You try to instruct customers that they should be selective and should not insert aluminum into the feed that comes into the plant."
Zelms stressed he was not suggesting the aluminum was added intentionally.
The Doe Run outtage comes as U.S. lead demand is set to pick up due to the battery making season getting underway and the onset of cold weather which causes lead acid auto batteries to fail.
The shutdown of Anvil Range Mining's Faro lead and zinc mine will also have a bullish effect on lead prices, analysts have said.
Zelms expected lead prices to average 35 to 36 cents per pound next year.

However, Zelms said although Doe Run was running flat out, the company was being offered lead from other suppliers and therefore it was purely speculative to say the company's outtage will prompt greater imports into the U.S., though a cold snap could encourage that.
